newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Stocks in Thailand, Korea swing wildly.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Stocks in Thailand, Korea swing wildly.

text.p: Thailand is about to assume Korea's position as the worst-performing stock market in Asia.

After months of bullish words but little buying, fund managers started pouring money into Korean stocks last week, lifting the KOSPI off a 35-month low. But in Thailand, the pendulum swung stocks in the opposite direction.

A series of political and economic woes hammered Thailand's SET index down to three digits on Friday for the first time in three years. It rose back above key support at 1,000 after a private sector rescue fund rushed to buy, and closed at 1007.51.

Thailand's central bank intervened with billions of dollars on the foreign exchange market on Friday after denying rumors, started in Singapore, of a looming devaluation. Meanwhile, rumors of brokerages being hit by client defaults on margin loans battered Thai stocks, prompting the 15.7 billion baht ($US628 million) rescue by the private sector rescue fund.
"If sentiment deteriorates even further, not even 10 rescue funds will save the market," warned Stephen Leung, chief investment officer at BZW Asia.

There are few signs Korea is benefitting at Thailand's expense, apart from changes to Morgan Stanley Capital International's indices. Most Asian markets were required to give ground to make way for Korea, whose Asian index weighting doubled to eight percent from four percent, and Taiwan, which was included for the first time effective September 2.

Fund managers said foreigners have funnelled US$3.5 billion into Korean stocks so far, but an 18-percent limit on foreign investment disguised their market presence until buying became particularly pronounced last week.
"We've suddenly seen very strong foreign money come in," said Abihijit Chakrabortti, regional strategist with Lehman Brothers.
A 35-month low close of 753.35 on August 28 stimulated serious interest on August 29, helping to bounce South Korean stocks back to end Friday at 784.05.

Asian market experts have been watching for a market bottom in Korea for weeks, as a slowing economy, poor half-year corporate earnings, political uncertainties and a widening trade deficit kept investors sidelined.
The jury is still out on whether last week's recovery is sustainable, partly because domestic investors continue to shun equities in favour of higher-yielding corporate paper.

"We think it's been overplayed, and on a relative valuation basis, Korea looks like one of the cheaper markets in Asia," said Chakrabortti. "But some of that value could be in doubt because there could still be more earnings disappointment."
Fund managers now seem to be playing the waiting game in Thailand, which was hit by a downgrade of its sovereign short-term debt rating by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
As forecast in an ING Barings report one week ago, the rating downgrade prompted rumours of a baht devaluation, requiring more official denials and central bank intervention.
Once again, the Asian view of the situation differed from that offered by North American experts.

"The central bank has handled the situation extremely effectively and in a more far-reaching manner than the aftermath of the peso crisis," ING Barings said, rejecting non-Asian comparisons to Mexico's 1994 cash and currency crisis.

Leung said consumer goods accounted for 80 percent of Mexico's imports prior to the 1994 crisis, while 70 percent of Thailand's imports are investment related and backed by substantial foreign reserves.
Foreign fund managers said the market will take its cue from a no-confidence vote in the prime minister on September 18, but the market could gyrate wildly beforehand.
If the no-confidence vote succeeds, parliament will have to be dissolved an a general election called, which would prompt a sudden rally in stocks and lower interest rate yields, ING Barings said.
